It serves as a fundamental methodology in the field of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). With the ongoing development of foundation models, there is a growing interest in exploring their abilities in reasoning tasks. In this paper, we introduce seminal foundation models proposed or adaptable for reasoning, highlighting the latest advancements in various reasoning tasks, methods, and benchmarks. We then delve into the potential future directions behind the emergence of reasoning abilities within foundation models. We also discuss the relevance of multimodal learning, autonomous agents, and super alignment in the context of reasoning. \"raw_source_name\": \"Data-Centric Engineering\", \"raw_type\": \"journal-article\"}, \"abstract\": \"Abstract This article proposes a framework of linked software agents that continuously interact with an underlying knowledge graph to automatically assess the impacts of potential flooding events. It builds on the idea of connected digital twins based on the World Avatar dynamic knowledge graph to create a semantically rich asset of data, knowledge, and computational capabilities accessible to humans, applications, and artificial intelligence. We develop three new ontologies to describe and link environmental measurements and their respective reporting stations, flood events, and their potential impact on population and built infrastructure as well as the built environment of a city itself. These coupled ontologies are deployed to dynamically instantiate near real-time data from multiple fragmented sources into the World Avatar. Sequences of autonomous agents connected via the derived information framework automatically assess consequences of newly instantiated data, such as newly raised flood warnings, and cascade respective updates through the graph to ensure up-to-date insights into the number of people and building stock value at risk. Although we showcase the strength of this technology in the context of flooding, our findings suggest that this system-of-systems approach is a promising solution to build holistic digital twins for various other contexts and use cases to support truly interoperable and smart cities.\"}, {\"id\": \"https://openalex.org/W2284332185\", \"doi\": null, \"title\": \"Using event calculus for normative reasoning of BDI agents in the context of norm identification\", \"publication_year\": 2015, \"type\": \"dissertation\", \"cited_by_count\": 0, \"open_access\": {\"is_oa\": true, \"oa_status\": \"green\", \"oa_url\": \"http://research.library.mun.ca/11653/1/thesis.pdf\", \"any_repository_has_fulltext\": true}, \"primary_location\": {\"id\": \"pmh:oai:research.library.mun.ca:11653\", \"doi\": null, \"is_oa\": true, \"landing_page_url\": \"http://research.library.mun.ca/11653/1/thesis.pdf\", \"pdf_url\": \"http://research.library.mun.ca/11653/1/thesis.pdf\", \"source\": {\"id\": \"https://openalex.org/S4306401319\", \"display_name\": \"Memorial University Research Repository (Memorial University)\", \"issn_l\": null, \"issn\": null, \"is_oa\": false, \"is_in_doaj\": false, \"is_core\": false, \"listed_in\": [], \"host_organization\": \"https://openalex.org/I130438778\", \"host_organization_name\": \"Memorial University of Newfoundland\", \"host_organization_lineage\": [\"https://openalex.org/I130438778\"], \"host_organization_lineage_names\": [], \"type\": \"repository\"}, \"license\": null, \"license_id\": null, \"version\": \"submittedVersion\", \"is_accepted\": false, \"is_published\": false, \"raw_source_name\": \"\", \"raw_type\": \"Thesis\"}, \"abstract\": \"In human society, where different backgrounds, cultures and objectives coexist, \\\\nnorms help predict, control and coordinate individual behavior. Similarly, norms have \\\\nbeen used in multi-agent systems to describe ideal behaviour for software agents. In \\\\nspite of this, agents are still expected behave autonomously, due to the leeway allowed \\\\nby norms as soft constraints on individual behavior. Existing work dealing with norm \\\\nidentification in multi-agent systems generally assumes that agents are fully aware of \\\\nall norms, either at design time or as a result of communication with other agents. \\\\nSimilarly, work examining the impact of norms in agent decision-making proposes \\\\nstrategies that assume agents have complete knowledge of normative states. \\\\nThis thesis proposes that agents do not have complete knowledge about normative \\\\nstates; consequently, it is the agents’ duty to identify norms. To this end, we \\\\npropose an agent architecture and algorithms for identifying dynamic permission and \\\\nprohibition norms in open multi-agent systems. Using Event Calculus, we propose \\\\na formal representation of norms and a normative practical reasoning mechanism. \\\\nOther studies assume that the normative states that are neither identified prohibited \\\\nnor obliged are permitted. Central to our proposal is that a normative state can be \\\\nunknown if it is not explicitly identified as prohibited, obliged or permitted. This \\\\nallows us to integrate permission norms into our proposed normative practical reasoning \\\\nmechanism. Thus, the contribution of this thesis is a set of techniques and \\\\nalgorithms that allow agents to join and function in a society regulated by (possibly \\\\nunknown) norms, while minimizing
